title: Bandwidth-aware microkernel profiler and adaptive selector for mixed-seqlen workloads
creator: Asha Menon
description: Problem: Our current kernel selection focuses primarily on latency and theoretical FLOP costs. In production traces with mixed short and long sequences, we observe suboptimal GPU memory bandwidth utilization and expensive kernel switching during prefill->decode transitions. Goal: Build a lightweight microkernel profiler that measures effective bandwidth and memory traffic characteristics per kernel variant (attention/layout/quantization combination) on real hardware, and an adaptive selector that uses these signals plus seqlen histograms and recent KV cache patterns to pick kernels that minimize tail latency and token cost for mixed workloads.
acceptance_criteria: 1) Microkernel profiler runs with <5% added overhead during sampling windows and reports per-kernel bandwidth metrics. 2) Adaptive selector integrated into runtime picks a kernel variant that reduces 95th percentile latency for mixed-seqlen synthetic workload by >=8% vs baseline. 3) No regression (>2%) in median latency for pure short-seq workloads. 4) Feature gated and rolloutable with metrics and canary checks in Console.
design_notes: High-level approach: 1) Lightweight sampling: instrument a small set of requests (configurable sample rate) to collect per-kernel counters: device memcpy throughput, kernel execution time, L2/DRAM estimated traffic (where available), and occupancy. 2) Normalize measurements to effective bandwidth used per token by dividing measured device traffic by tokens processed. 3) Build a microkernel performance model: model = base_latency + alpha*seqlen + beta*bandwidth_pressure + gamma*prefill_factor. Use linear models with piecewise buckets for seqlen. 4) Runtime decision: combine runtime model predictions with an exploration bonus (epsilon-decay) to allow discovering better kernels after env changes (driver updates, workload shift). 5) Integrate with prefill/decode scheduling: for prefill-heavy requests prefer kernels with higher sustained bandwidth; for decode-heavy low-latency requests prefer kernels with lower invocation overhead and better single-token latency. Trade-offs: sampling frequency vs overhead, model complexity vs stability, and how to weight historical telemetry vs fresh probes. Edge cases: on low-util hosts, bandwidth is not the bottleneck; selector should detect low contention and fallback to latency-optimized kernel.
progress_updates: 2025-01-12: Kickoff meeting with runtime, infra, and perf teams. Agreed on sampling hooks and privacy constraints. Action: Diego to prototype counters in runtime-agent.

2025-01-20: Prototype of kernel counter exports landed in internal branch (PR: github.com/redwood/runtime/pull/3421). Initial counters: kernel_ms, memcpy_bytes, tokens_processed. Observed ~3% overhead at 1% sample rate.

2025-01-28: Offline microbench run across instance types (g4dn, a100-p4) to map bandwidth regimes for three attention implementations. Results uploaded to Confluence: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RUNTIME/Microkernel+Bandwidth+Study

2025-02-03: Design review with PM and observability team. Feedback: include canary metrics in Console (per-route kernel_choice, kernel_bandwidth_utilization, decision_reason). Added a telemetry schema proposal.

2025-02-10: Implemented simple linear model and a small selector shim. End-to-end integration test shows 6% p95 improvement on mixed-seqlen synthetic workload. Remaining: exploration/decay and rollout automation.
2025-02-14: Security review request created (ticket SEC-2025-11) — no blockers expected. Planning canary for next sprint.
2025-02-15: Updated acceptance criteria to require <2% median regression for short-seq workloads per design feedback.
risks: Sampling overhead spikes under bursty loads if sample rate is misconfigured
Driver/hardware telemetry variance may produce noisy estimates, requiring smoothing or heavier regularization
Incorrect weighting can hurt median latency for critical short-seq requests if not gated properly
Rolling out the selector cluster-wide before adequate canarying could cause noisy customer-facing regressions
test_plan: Unit tests for counter exports and model code. Integration tests: 1) Synthetic mixed-seqlen harness with measured baselines; 2) Replay of production sampled traces under a staging cluster to validate decisions; 3) A/B canary where 10% traffic uses adaptive selector, with health checks for latency and error increases. Add chaos tests: simulate driver update that reduces bandwidth and verify selector adapts within N=1000 samples.
rollout_plan: Feature gated behind runtime flag 'adaptive_bandwidth_selector'. Staged rollout: local dev -> staging (full regression) -> Canary (10% traffic for 24h) -> Incremental ramp with automated rollback if p95 latency increases >5% or error rate increases >0.5%. Console metrics dashboard and alert playbook created.
monitoring: Expose per-route metrics: selected_kernel, kernel_bandwidth_utilization, est_tokens_per_ms, decision_confidence. Dashboards: kernel_bandwidth_trends, selector_exploration_rate. Alerts: p95 latency drift, sudden kernel churn, unexpected bandwidth drops.
next_steps: 1) Finish exploration-decay schedule and integrate with rollout orchestration (Due 2025-02-28). 2) Add L2/DRAM estimator where hardware supports it. 3) Run extended canary with diverse production routes.
notes_for_prod_support: If customers report latency regressions after enabling selector, immediately disable feature flag per-customer and capture profiler traces. Support playbook links and rollback runbook attached to Console playbook entry. Contact runtime on-call and tagging in PagerDuty.
observability_requirements: Add trace spans for 'kernel_selection_decision' with fields: chosen_variant, confidence_score, sampled_bandwidth, historic_bandwidth_mean. Retain sampling traces for 30 days under perf-retention tier.
final_notes: This ticket focuses on adding a new signal (effective bandwidth) to the kernel decision stack and proving end-to-end value for mixed workloads. The selector is intentionally conservative: it prefers safe fallbacks and will degrade exploration frequency when customer-impact risk is high.
changelog: 2025-01-10 created by Asha Menon; 2025-01-20 prototype PR; 2025-01-28 benchmark results uploaded; 2025-02-03 design review; 2025-02-10 initial selector prototype; 2025-02-15 acceptance criteria tightened.
